newsitem.title: USA: San Joaquin toll road may see rating cut -- report.
newsitem.headline: San Joaquin toll road may see rating cut -- report.

text.p: Larger-than-expected revenue shortfalls for the San Joaquin Hills, Calif., toll road may prompt a rating downgrade, but other factors mitigate the problem, J.P. Morgan Securities Inc. said in a new report.

J.P. Morgan, which has been selected as a co-senior manager on a proposed bond refunding by the toll road, said in the report that toll coverage is likely to fall below 1.1 times on senior lien bonds.
That might prompt Fitch Investors Service Inc to lower its BBB rating to BBB-minus, but probably not below investment grade, J.P. Morgan said.
"We do not think a sharp reduction in rating would be warranted without more hard data and a completely updated ... study, both of which require time to assemble," the report said.

Wilbur Smith Associates recently completed a preliminary analysis of the first three months of traffic on the toll road, concluding that transactions are likely to fall considerably short of forecasts prepared for the toll road's 1993 bond offering.

Last year, J.P. Morgan predicted the revenue shortfall would be about 15 percent, but based on the new data, the firm said it is more likely to be 25 percent lower and remain that way for the rest of the decade.

Wilbur Smith's report cited a substantially lower rate of economic growth as the principal reason for the toll road's performance so far. Other problems include road signage, and a new high occupancy vehicle lane on Interstate 5, which eased congestion on that competing highway.
J.P. Morgan stressed the toll road's poor signage, noting that signs on other roads refer to the toll road simply as "SJH Tollroad," without noting destinations.
"Barring regular commuters and bondholders, it is doubtful many others realize what this denotes," J.P. Morgan's report said.
J.P. Morgan said the toll road plans to fix the problem with its own funds, and the report noted that an expected increase in traffic heading into the summer should offset some of the revenue issues.

The firm's report said signage and problems related to ramp-up periods should resolve themselves. But "the larger shortfall caused by reduced economic growth and less traffic diversion is more troubling," the report says.
Employment in Orange County had been projected to grow about two percent annually between 1990 and 1995, and 2.6 percent between 1995 and 2000. Instead, employment was flat from 1990 to 1996.

"Since early 1996, though, the economic picture has improved considerably," the report said. "Employment in 1996 gained 2.6 percent which approximates the original forecast, and in the 12 months ended in January, employment rose 2.9 percent."
Despite all the early problems on the road, J.P. Morgan said the risk of any immediate payment problem for bondholders is "virtually nonexistent" since interest is capitalized into early 1999.
